## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Huṁhuṅka Sutta* (Ud 1.4; PTS Ud 3) is a discourse in the *Bodhivagga* of the *Udāna* [SuttaCentral]. Set on the bank of the river Nerañjarā, the narrative opens after the Buddha has spent seven continuous days seated in a single cross-legged position experiencing the bliss of liberation (*vimuttisukha*) [Masefield 1997]. Upon emerging from that meditative absorption, he is approached by a haughty brahmin characterized as of the "Huṁhuṅka" breed (*humhuṅkajātiko*), an epithet denoting one who recites or utters the sound *huṁ* [SuttaCentral; Masefield 1997]. The visitor inquires about what makes someone a genuine brahmin, prompting the Buddha to deliver an inspired utterance (*udāna*) defining the qualities of the true brahmin [SuttaCentral; Masefield 1997].

In terms of parallels and text reuse, SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus agree on a direct alignment between this sutta and the opening narrative of the Vinaya Piṭaka's *Mahākhandhaka* (Kd 1; segments §1.4–4.5 matching Kd 1 §2.1.1_2–2.3.6) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. Further verse parallels are preserved in the Sanskrit and Tibetan *Udānavarga* traditions within their respective chapters on the brahmin (UV 33, UVS 33, and Uv Kg 33) [SuttaCentral]. A related account of this encounter is also found in the Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit *Mahāvastu* (iii 325) [Masefield 1997], and the discourse is referenced in the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 37) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus detects additional Pali-internal reuse across twenty-eight texts, sharing stock narrative and doctrinal phrasing with the *Dasakanipāta* (AN 10), *Chakkanipāta* (AN 6), *Māra Saṁyutta* (SN 4), and neighboring *Udāna* suttas (Ud 1.1, Ud 2.1, and Ud 3.10) [DharmaNexus]. Modern translations include sixteen renderings across thirteen languages listed on SuttaCentral, including English versions by Bhikkhu Sujato and Peter Masefield [SuttaCentral; Masefield 1997].
